lessons.title: Normal Pregnancy: Physiological Changes and Antenatal Assessment
lessons.lay_summary: Pregnancy causes profound changes in every body system. Understanding what is normal helps nurses identify what is abnormal.

content.intro: Pregnancy induces systematic physiological adaptations to support foetal growth and prepare for labour. These changes affect cardiovascular, respiratory, haematological, renal, gastrointestinal, and musculoskeletal systems. Recognising normal physiological changes prevents over-investigation and ensures genuine complications are not missed.

sections.title: Cardiovascular and Haematological Changes
sections.body: Blood volume increases 40-50% by 32 weeks (plasma > red cell mass → physiological anaemia of pregnancy — Hb 10.5-11 g/dL is normal at term). Cardiac output increases 30-50% (↑ HR + ↑ stroke volume). Blood pressure: falls in first and second trimester (progesterone-mediated vasodilatation), returns to baseline by term. A BP rise above baseline in the third trimester is clinically significant. Heart rate: increases 10-20 bpm above baseline. Coagulation: hypercoagulable state (↑ fibrinogen, factors VII, VIII, X; ↓ protein S) — VTE risk ×5 vs non-pregnant. Physiological leucocytosis up to 12,000/μL is normal.

sections.title: Respiratory and Renal Changes
sections.body: Respiratory: progesterone stimulates the respiratory centre → ↑ tidal volume (40%), ↑ minute ventilation, respiratory alkalosis (pCO2 ~30 mmHg normal in pregnancy). Dyspnoea in early-mid pregnancy is often physiological. Elevated diaphragm (by uterus) → ↓ functional residual capacity. Renal: GFR increases 50% by second trimester → serum creatinine and urea fall; values 'normal' outside pregnancy may indicate impairment in pregnancy (Cr >75 μmol/L, urea >4.5 mmol/L warrant investigation). Glycosuria is common (lower renal glucose threshold) — does not diagnose gestational diabetes. Ureteric dilatation (progesterone effect + uterine compression) → increased UTI risk.

sections.title: Standard Antenatal Assessment
sections.body: WHO 2016 recommends minimum 8 antenatal contacts. First visit assessment: confirm pregnancy (hCG), baseline BP, weight/BMI, blood group and Rh, FBC (anaemia), rubella immunity, STI screen (HIV, syphilis, HBV, HCV, chlamydia), urine culture (screen for asymptomatic bacteriuria), HbA1c or OGTT (diabetes risk), Down's syndrome screening (combined first trimester: nuchal translucency + PAPP-A + beta-hCG at 11-13+6 weeks). At every visit: BP, urinalysis (protein), foetal heart rate (Doppler from 12 weeks), symphysis-fundal height (SFH from 24 weeks — cm ≈ gestational weeks ±3).

sections.title: Rhesus (Rh) Incompatibility and Anti-D Prophylaxis
sections.body: Rh-negative mothers (15% of population) are at risk of sensitisation if they carry an Rh-positive foetus. Sensitisation occurs when foetal RBCs cross the placenta (sensitising events: bleeding, amniocentesis, ectopic pregnancy, miscarriage, delivery). Once sensitised, subsequent Rh-positive pregnancies: maternal IgG anti-D crosses placenta → haemolytic disease of the foetus/newborn (HDFN) — hydrops fetalis, kernicterus, stillbirth. Prevention: anti-D immunoglobulin (Rho(D) Immune Globulin / RhoGAM): given IM within 72 hours of sensitising event AND routinely at 28-30 weeks gestation (UK: 500 IU at 28+34 weeks). Anti-D works by destroying foetal RBCs before maternal immune sensitisation occurs.

content.clinical_pearl: Supine hypotension syndrome: after 20 weeks, the gravid uterus compresses the inferior vena cava when the mother lies flat → ↓ venous return → ↓ cardiac output → dizziness, nausea, pre-syncope. Treat by positioning in left lateral decubitus (tilts uterus off IVC). Always position pregnant patients beyond 20 weeks in left lateral tilt for procedures.
key_points: Physiological anaemia of pregnancy: Hb 10.5-11 g/dL acceptable; plasma volume rises more than RBC mass
Serum creatinine is lower in pregnancy; 'normal' values may indicate impairment
Anti-D prophylaxis: within 72h of sensitising event + routine at 28-30 weeks for Rh-negative women
VTE risk is ×5 in pregnancy — assess risk at booking and each contact
Supine hypotension >20 weeks: left lateral tilt relieves IVC compression
references: WHO. WHO recommendations on antenatal care for a positive pregnancy experience. WHO, 2016
NICE. Guideline NG201: Antenatal care. NICE, 2021
RCOG. Green-top guideline No. 22: Use of Anti-D Immunoglobulin for Rhesus D Prophylaxis. 2011

lessons.title: Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy
lessons.lay_summary: Pre-eclampsia is a leading cause of maternal and perinatal mortality worldwide. Early recognition and prompt management save lives.

content.intro: Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy affect 5-10% of pregnancies globally and are a leading cause of maternal and perinatal mortality. The spectrum includes: chronic hypertension (pre-existing), gestational hypertension (new onset ≥20 weeks without proteinuria), pre-eclampsia, and eclampsia. The 2023 ACOG guidance redefines pre-eclampsia criteria to include severe features even without proteinuria.

sections.title: Diagnostic Criteria for Pre-eclampsia
sections.body: Blood pressure: ≥140/90 mmHg on two occasions ≥4 hours apart after 20 weeks gestation (previously normotensive). PLUS any of: proteinuria ≥300 mg/24h or PCR ≥30 mg/mmol; OR severe features even without proteinuria. Severe features: BP ≥160/110 mmHg, thrombocytopaenia (<100,000/μL), renal insufficiency (Cr >96 μmol/L), impaired liver function (ALT/AST >2× upper limit), new-onset headache not responding to analgesia, pulmonary oedema, visual disturbance. HELLP syndrome (variant): Haemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets — associated with high maternal mortality.

sections.title: Nursing Assessment and Monitoring
sections.body: At every antenatal contact: BP (correct technique: seated, arm at heart level, correct cuff size, 2 readings 2 minutes apart, use lower reading), urinalysis (protein dipstick → 2+ or more requires formal quantification). Assess for symptoms: headache (frontal, severe, not relieved by paracetamol), visual disturbance (flashing lights — scotomata, blurring), epigastric/RUQ pain (hepatic capsule stretching), nausea/vomiting, facial/hand oedema (sudden). Daily: assess DTRs (deep tendon reflexes) — hyperreflexia indicates CNS irritability. Foetal assessment: CTG, growth scan (IUGR common), liquor volume.

sections.title: Management and Antihypertensive Therapy
sections.body: Mild-moderate hypertension (140-159/90-109): labetalol (first-line, oral), nifedipine (slow-release), methyldopa. Severe hypertension (≥160/110): treat within 30-60 minutes — IV labetalol (bolus then infusion), oral nifedipine (immediate-release), IV hydralazine. Target: 130-150/80-100 mmHg (avoid overcorrection → placental ischaemia). Magnesium sulphate: for seizure prophylaxis in severe pre-eclampsia and treatment of eclampsia. Loading dose: 4 g IV over 20 minutes; maintenance: 1 g/h infusion. Monitor for magnesium toxicity: loss of patellar reflexes (first sign → stop infusion), respiratory depression (RR <12/min), cardiac arrest. Antidote: calcium gluconate 1 g IV.

sections.title: Eclampsia Management
sections.body: Eclampsia = new-onset grand mal seizures in a woman with pre-eclampsia (or without prior diagnosis). Medical emergency. ABCDE assessment: position left lateral, maintain airway (recovery position, do not insert biting block), oxygen, IV access. Magnesium sulphate: if not already started — load 4 g IV over 5-10 minutes; if on maintenance and re-seizures → 2 g bolus. Monitor foetal heart rate after maternal stabilisation. Plan delivery: after maternal stabilisation, delivery is the only cure — mode depends on cervical favourability and foetal status. Post-partum: pre-eclampsia/eclampsia can occur up to 6 weeks post-delivery; BP monitoring essential post-discharge.

content.clinical_pearl: The patellar reflex is your real-time magnesium toxicity monitor. Check reflexes before each dose of maintenance MgSO4. If reflexes are absent — stop the infusion. Respiratory depression follows loss of reflexes. Keep calcium gluconate at the bedside whenever MgSO4 is running.
key_points: Pre-eclampsia: BP ≥140/90 after 20 weeks + proteinuria or severe features
Severe hypertension (≥160/110) must be treated within 30-60 minutes to prevent stroke
MgSO4: 4 g loading dose; toxicity — absent reflexes → respiratory depression; antidote = calcium gluconate 1 g IV
HELLP: Haemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets — high maternal mortality
Pre-eclampsia can develop/worsen up to 6 weeks post-partum
references: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 222: Gestational Hypertension and Preeclampsia. Obstetrics & Gynecology, 2020
NICE. Guideline NG133: Hypertension in pregnancy. NICE, 2019 updated 2023
Magee LA et al. CHIPS Trial — tight vs less tight BP control. NEJM 2015;372:407-417

lessons.title: Preterm Labour and Fetal Surveillance
lessons.lay_summary: Preterm birth before 37 weeks is the leading cause of neonatal death. Nurses must recognise early signs, initiate appropriate monitoring, and support families.

content.intro: Preterm birth (PTB) occurs in 5-18% of pregnancies worldwide and is the leading cause of neonatal morbidity and mortality. Gestational age at delivery is the primary determinant of outcome: <28 weeks (extremely preterm) carries the highest mortality; 28-32 weeks (very preterm); 32-37 weeks (moderate to late preterm). Nursing care focuses on recognition, corticosteroid administration, tocolysis decisions, and foetal wellbeing monitoring.

sections.title: Recognising Preterm Labour
sections.body: Preterm labour (PTL) = regular uterine contractions (≥4 in 20 minutes or ≥8 in 60 minutes) with progressive cervical change before 37 weeks. Symptoms: low back pain (constant or rhythmic), pelvic pressure, menstrual-like cramping, vaginal discharge or bleeding, rupture of membranes. Assessment: cervical length on transvaginal ultrasound (<25 mm at 24 weeks indicates high risk), fetal fibronectin (fFN) test (high negative predictive value — if negative, delivery within 2 weeks very unlikely), CTG for contraction pattern and foetal wellbeing, urinalysis (UTI is a common precipitant — treat immediately).

sections.title: Antenatal Corticosteroids (ACS)
sections.body: ACS significantly reduce neonatal morbidity and mortality by accelerating foetal lung maturation. Indication: threatened PTL between 24-34+6 weeks. Standard regimen: betamethasone 12 mg IM × 2 doses 24 hours apart (or dexamethasone 6 mg IM × 4 doses 12 hours apart). Maximum benefit: 24 hours to 7 days after first dose. Benefit beyond 34 weeks is debated. Nursing: administer promptly when ordered (every hour of delay reduces benefit), document time of each dose, monitor maternal blood glucose (corticosteroids cause transient hyperglycaemia — especially significant in diabetic pregnancies), prepare NICU team if delivery appears imminent.

sections.title: Cardiotocography (CTG) Interpretation Essentials
sections.body: CTG monitors: foetal heart rate (FHR) baseline, variability, accelerations, decelerations. Normal (reassuring): baseline 110-160 bpm, variability 5-25 bpm, ≥2 accelerations in 20 min (15 bpm × 15 seconds), no decelerations. Variability: normal indicates intact CNS-cardiac axis. Reduced variability (<5 bpm for >50 min) is most sensitive indicator of foetal compromise. Accelerations: reassuring — absence alone is not pathological. Decelerations: Early (mirror contractions — benign, head compression); Variable (cord compression — occur at any point relative to contractions); Late (placental insufficiency — begin after contraction peak, most concerning). NICE FIGO classification: normal, suspicious, pathological — pathological CTG → action required.

sections.title: Non-Stress Test (NST) and Biophysical Profile (BPP)
sections.body: NST: monitors FHR for 20-40 minutes. Reactive NST: ≥2 accelerations of ≥15 bpm lasting ≥15 seconds in 20 minutes (indicates foetal wellbeing). Non-reactive NST (<2 accelerations): requires further assessment (vibroacoustic stimulation, BPP, biophysical assessment). BPP: combines NST + ultrasound assessment of 4 parameters: foetal movement (≥3 discrete body/limb movements in 30 min), foetal tone (≥1 extension/flexion), foetal breathing movements (≥1 episode of ≥30 seconds in 30 min), amniotic fluid volume (deepest vertical pocket ≥2 cm). Score: 2 points each if normal. Score 8/8 (or 8/10 with normal AFI): reassuring; ≤4: delivery usually indicated.

content.clinical_pearl: Magnesium sulphate for neuroprotection: at <32 weeks, MgSO4 given before anticipated preterm birth reduces cerebral palsy in survivors by ~30%. This is a different indication from eclampsia prophylaxis but the same drug. Ensure the order is present and administered before delivery when PTB <32 weeks is expected.
key_points: PTL: ≥4 contractions/20 min + cervical change before 37 weeks; rule out UTI
Corticosteroids (betamethasone 12 mg IM × 2): optimal benefit 24h-7 days after first dose; give immediately when indicated
CTG: normal variability 5-25 bpm; late decelerations = placental insufficiency = most concerning
Reactive NST: ≥2 accelerations (15 bpm × 15s) in 20 minutes
MgSO4 <32 weeks: neuroprotection — reduces cerebral palsy by ~30%
references: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 171: Management of Preterm Labor. Obstetrics & Gynecology, 2016
WHO. Antenatal corticosteroids for improving outcomes. WHO Recommendation, 2022
NICE. Guideline NG25: Preterm labour and birth. NICE, 2015 updated 2022

flashcards.question: Pre-eclampsia diagnostic criteria?
flashcards.answer: BP ≥140/90 mmHg on 2 occasions ≥4h apart, after 20 weeks + proteinuria ≥300mg/24h or PCR ≥30, OR severe features (thrombocytopenia, renal/hepatic dysfunction, pulmonary oedema, visual disturbance, severe headache).

flashcards.question: MgSO4 toxicity: signs in order and antidote?
flashcards.answer: First: loss of patellar reflex → respiratory depression (RR <12) → cardiac arrest. Antidote: calcium gluconate 1g IV.

flashcards.question: Antenatal corticosteroid regimen and indication?
flashcards.answer: Betamethasone 12mg IM × 2 doses 24h apart (or dexamethasone 6mg IM × 4 doses 12h apart). Indicated for threatened PTL at 24-34+6 weeks. Maximum benefit 24h-7 days post first dose.

flashcards.question: Anti-D prophylaxis: when and why?
flashcards.answer: Rh-negative mothers: within 72h of sensitising event (bleeding, amniocentesis, delivery) + routine at 28-30 weeks. Prevents maternal sensitisation that would cause HDFN in future pregnancies.

mcq_questions.question: A patient at 32 weeks gestation presents with sudden-onset bright red, painless vaginal bleeding. The nurse's PRIORITY action is:

options.A: Perform a vaginal exam to assess cervical dilation
options.B: Place the patient in left lateral position and apply fetal monitor

mcq_questions.explanation: Painless bright red bleeding at 32 weeks is placenta previa until proven otherwise. Vaginal exams are CONTRAINDICATED (can cause catastrophic haemorrhage). Priority: left lateral positioning (relieve aortocaval compression), continuous fetal monitoring, IV access, type and crossmatch, call provider. Diagnosis confirmed by ultrasound. Emergency C-section if haemodynamically unstable.

mcq_questions.question: A primigravida at 38 weeks has BP 158/105 mmHg, 3+ proteinuria, and reports persistent severe headache and visual changes. Which diagnosis and intervention are CORRECT?

options.A: Gestational hypertension — start oral nifedipine and monitor
options.B: Severe preeclampsia — initiate IV magnesium sulfate and prepare for delivery
options.D: Mild preeclampsia — bed rest and repeat labs in 1 week

mcq_questions.explanation: Severe preeclampsia criteria (ACOG): BP ≥160/110 on two readings, severe symptoms (headache, visual changes, epigastric pain), plus proteinuria. IV magnesium sulfate 4-6g loading dose is given for seizure prophylaxis. Definitive treatment is delivery. Magnesium toxicity signs: loss of DTRs (first sign), RR <12, urinary output <25mL/hr. Calcium gluconate is the antidote.

mcq_questions.question: A nurse is administering IV magnesium sulfate to a preeclamptic patient. Which finding requires the nurse to STOP the infusion immediately?

options.B: Absent deep tendon reflexes and respiratory rate 10/min

mcq_questions.explanation: Absent DTRs (earliest clinical sign of toxicity) + RR <12 indicate severe magnesium toxicity. Stop infusion immediately and prepare calcium gluconate 1g IV (antidote). Therapeutic range: 4–7 mg/dL (2–3.5 mEq/L). Toxic: DTR loss at 7–10 mg/dL; respiratory arrest at 10–13 mg/dL. Mild flushing is an expected side effect, not toxicity.

mcq_questions.question: A patient at 28 weeks is diagnosed with gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM). Which dietary instruction is CORRECT?

options.B: Distribute carbohydrate intake evenly across 3 meals and 2–3 snacks daily
options.C: Eliminate all fruit and dairy from the diet
options.D: Follow the same diet as a non-pregnant diabetic patient

mcq_questions.explanation: ADA/ACOG recommendation: consistent carbohydrate distribution (175g/day minimum in pregnancy), not elimination. Three meals and 2-3 snacks prevent post-meal glucose spikes and fasting hypoglycaemia. Morning carbohydrate is limited (insulin resistance is highest in the morning). Blood glucose targets: fasting <95 mg/dL; 1-hr postprandial <140 mg/dL. Most GDM is managed with diet/exercise first.

mcq_questions.question: Which assessment finding in a postpartum patient at 12 hours after vaginal delivery requires IMMEDIATE nursing action?

options.A: Fundus firm, at umbilicus, slightly right of midline
options.B: Saturating one perineal pad per hour for 3 consecutive hours

mcq_questions.explanation: Saturating >1 pad/hour is abnormal postpartum bleeding (PPH). Primary PPH occurs in the first 24 hours; most common cause is uterine atony. IMMEDIATE assessment: uterine tone (boggy uterus → fundal massage), bladder distension (full bladder displaces fundus, causes atony), vital signs. Notify provider, establish IV access, administer oxytocin. A single temperature of 37.8°C is not immediately concerning.

mcq_questions.question: A nurse is teaching a breastfeeding patient about mastitis. Which statement by the patient indicates INCORRECT understanding?

options.A: "I should continue breastfeeding even when I have mastitis"
options.B: "I need to stop breastfeeding immediately to let my breast heal"
options.C: "I should complete the full antibiotic course even if I feel better"
options.D: "Applying warm compresses before feeding may help drainage"

mcq_questions.explanation: Mastitis is an infection of breast tissue common in the first 6 weeks postpartum. WHO and ABM guidelines recommend CONTINUING breastfeeding (or pumping) — emptying the breast is therapeutic and does not harm the infant. Stopping breastfeeding increases risk of abscess formation. Treatment: antistaphylococcal antibiotics (dicloxacillin/cephalexin), supportive care, and continued emptying.

mcq_questions.question: A patient at 36 weeks presents with severe abdominal pain described as 'tearing,' a rigid board-like abdomen, and minimal vaginal bleeding. Fetal heart tones are 80 bpm. This presentation is MOST consistent with:
mcq_questions.explanation: Placental abruption: sudden severe abdominal pain, rigid abdomen, dark vaginal bleeding (or concealed), fetal distress. Fetal bradycardia (80 bpm) indicates fetal compromise. This is an obstetric emergency: emergency C-section. Risk factors: hypertension, cocaine use, trauma, prior abruption. Distinct from placenta previa (painless bright red bleeding). DIC can complicate severe abruption.

mcq_questions.question: Which Rh-related nursing intervention is required for an Rh-negative mother who delivers an Rh-positive infant?

options.A: Administer Rh immunoglobulin (RhoGAM) within 72 hours of delivery
options.B: No intervention is needed after delivery if RhoGAM was given at 28 weeks
options.C: Give the infant RhoGAM to prevent haemolysis
options.D: Perform exchange transfusion on the newborn

mcq_questions.explanation: Postpartum RhoGAM (300 mcg IM) must be given within 72 hours to an Rh-negative mother who delivers an Rh-positive infant. RhoGAM at 28 weeks is antenatal prophylaxis — postpartum dose is still required. Without it, the mother develops anti-D antibodies that attack Rh-positive fetuses in future pregnancies (erythroblastosis fetalis). RhoGAM is given to the mother, not the infant.

mcq_questions.question: A patient who delivered 4 days ago calls the clinic reporting feeling 'sad and tearful' and occasionally overwhelmed. She is sleeping and eating adequately and is caring for her infant. This MOST likely represents:

options.B: Postpartum blues — a normal, self-limiting condition
options.D: Normal adjustment that requires no follow-up

mcq_questions.explanation: Postpartum blues affect 50–75% of mothers, beginning day 2–3 and resolving by day 10–14 without treatment. Symptoms: tearfulness, mood swings, anxiety — while maintaining functional ability. Postpartum depression (PPD) persists >2 weeks, impairs functioning, and requires SSRI ± therapy. Postpartum psychosis is rare, rapid-onset (<72 hrs), with delusions/hallucinations — a psychiatric emergency. Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) screens at 2-week and 6-week visits.

mcq_questions.question: A primigravida at 41 weeks undergoes labour induction with misoprostol (Cytotec). Twenty minutes after insertion, the fetal monitor shows a 7-minute contraction with late decelerations. The nurse's FIRST action is:

options.B: Remove the misoprostol insert and prepare for tocolysis
options.C: Administer oxygen at 10L/min via non-rebreather mask

mcq_questions.explanation: Tachysystole (>5 contractions in 10 min) with late decelerations indicates uterine hyperstimulation causing uteroplacental insufficiency. For misoprostol: remove the vaginal insert immediately. For oxytocin: stop infusion. Then: lateral positioning, IV fluid bolus, supplemental oxygen. Tocolysis (terbutaline 0.25mg SQ) may be needed if tachysystole persists. NEVER increase oxytocin when tachysystole is occurring.

mcq_questions.question: Which TORCH infection transmitted during pregnancy causes periventricular calcifications and chorioretinitis in the newborn?
mcq_questions.explanation: Congenital CMV is the most common congenital infection and the leading infectious cause of hearing loss and neurodevelopmental disability. Classic findings: periventricular calcifications, chorioretinitis, microcephaly, sensorineural hearing loss. CMV is transmitted via urine, saliva, breast milk. Toxoplasmosis causes diffuse intracranial calcifications. Rubella causes cataracts, cardiac defects, deafness (congenital rubella syndrome). HSV causes encephalitis.

mcq_questions.question: A patient at 20 weeks is newly diagnosed with placenta previa. She is asymptomatic. The nurse should educate her to AVOID:

options.B: Pelvic rest — no sexual intercourse, vaginal exams, or tampons

mcq_questions.explanation: Placenta previa (placenta covering the cervical os) requires pelvic rest: no vaginal intercourse, vaginal exams, or anything inserted into the vagina. These can trigger catastrophic haemorrhage by disturbing the placenta overlying the os. Many placenta previas resolve by 28–32 weeks as the lower uterine segment develops. Ultrasound follow-up at 28-32 weeks is standard. Iron supplementation is recommended due to haemorrhage risk.
